body:
FOUND BY FIXING A TEST, 2026-08-19. rails-guard refused a skipped rail; replacing the skip with a
true assertion exposed a live disclosure.

MEASURED, on the ordinary query door, after a deliberate administrative act:

    BEFORE DROP: {"alice_Plant":{"height":11}}    <- the peer's claim, correctly scoped
    AFTER  DROP: {"alice_Plant":{"height":999}}   <- the RECEIVER's own private claim

Severing a channel purges its pool and negates its channel record, but leaves the LAW it blessed
registered in the receiver's ground. `channelGroundFor` looks a channel up by prefix among LIVE
channels, finds none, and returns undefined — so the read falls through to the primary ground. A name
that answered a peer now answers you, with no error and nothing in the report.

It is the same shape as T193's subscription leak and arguably worse: it is the ordinary read path,
it follows an act the operator chose, and it looks like it worked.

FIXED BY FAILING CLOSED. `channelsEver` reads severed channels too, so the read path can tell a name
that was NEVER a channel (an ordinary lens) from one whose channel is GONE (a lens with no ground).
The second refuses and says why. A refusal is always available; a wrong answer that looks right is
not recoverable.

WHAT IS NOT DECIDED, and is Myk's: SHOULD A DROP RETIRE THE LENSES IT BLESSED? Failing closed leaves
the binding registered and unreadable, which is honest but odd — `federate list` no longer shows the
channel while the lens is still in the store's registry. Retiring them on drop would be tidier and is
a WIDENING of what drop removes: today it purges a pool's bytes, and that would add the receiver's
own bindings. Under the erasure rule that is Myk's merge with its one-line statement of what can now
be deleted that could not before.

RAILS: the drop rail now asserts the refusal by name, and the two-sided case (a bystander channel's
lens still serves) sits beside it.
title: A severed channel's lens fell back to the receiver's own ground
